title: Realtor Bio Examples: How to Write One People Want to Meet
summary: Realtor bio examples and a simple five-part formula for a bio that sounds like a person, plus the right length for your site, Zillow and Instagram.
body_markdown:
Most realtor bios sound the same. "Top-producing, results-driven agent with a passion for real estate and a commitment to exceptional service." Swap the name and it fits a hundred agents in the same zip code.


A Chicago brokerage leader we talked with described the bio they want visitors to read: one that makes them think, "that's someone I can go ahead and have a piece of pizza with." No stats, no sales volume. Just enough about the person that a stranger wants to meet them.


Your bio is the page where someone decides if they like you. This guide gives you a formula, five examples and the right length for each place your bio lives.


**Fast facts:**


-


People pick an agent they trust and like. Your bio should help with both.


-


Lead with who you are and who you help. Put credentials last, or leave them out.


-


One specific, memorable detail beats a list of hobbies.


-


Write a long version for your website and LinkedIn, and a short one for Instagram (150 characters) and your Zillow or Google profiles.


-


Read it out loud. If you wouldn't say it at a barbecue, cut it.


*Image: Your bio brings people in. Remembering them is what keeps them.*


## The five-part bio formula


Every bio below follows the same shape. Use it as a checklist, not a script.


Part


What it answers


Example line


1. Who you are


Name, where you live, how long


"I'm Dana, and I've lived in Oak Park for 14 years."


2. Who you help


The people you're best for


"I mostly help first-time buyers who are nervous about the whole thing."


3. One real detail


Something they'll remember you by


"I coach my daughter's softball team and lose most of the games."


4. How you work


What it's like to hire you


"I'll text you back fast, and I'll tell you when a house isn't worth it."


5. How to reach you


An easy next step


"Text me at the number below. Coffee's on me."


The detail in part 3 does the most work. It gives a stranger something to mention when they call ("You're the softball coach!"), and that's how a relationship starts.


## Five realtor bio examples


These agents are made up. Borrow the structure, not the details.


**The first-time buyer specialist**


"I'm Dana Ruiz. I've lived in Oak Park for 14 years and bought my first condo here when I was 26, terrified and sure I'd done everything wrong. Now I mostly help first-time buyers who feel the way I did. I coach my daughter's softball team, badly. I'll explain every step before it happens, text you back fast, and tell you honestly when a house isn't worth it. Text me any time."


**The career changer**


"Before real estate I taught eighth-grade science for 11 years, which turns out to be good training for explaining inspection reports. I help buyers and sellers on the north side of Milwaukee, and I'm happiest with people who want to understand the process, not just get through it. Ask me about my sourdough starter. Or ask me about your house."


**The neighborhood expert**


"I grew up three blocks from where I live now, in Logan Square. I know which streets flood, which coffee shop has the good window seat and which blocks are quiet on Saturday nights. If you're buying or selling here, I'll tell you what the listing photos won't. I've sold homes in this neighborhood for nine years, and most of my clients come from other clients."


**The downsizing and estate specialist**


"Most of my clients are selling a house they've lived in for 30 years, or one a parent left them. That's a lot more than a transaction, and I don't rush it. I'll help you find the right estate sale company, the right movers and the right price, in that order. I'm a grandmother of four and a terrible golfer. Call me and we'll talk it through."


**The investor-friendly agent**


"I own four rental units myself, so I run the numbers the way you will: rent, taxes, repairs, vacancy. I work with investors buying two- to four-unit buildings on the south side and with owners ready to sell. I'm direct, I answer my phone, and I'll tell you when a deal doesn't pencil out. Off the clock I'm usually at a Sox game."


## How long your bio should be, by platform


The same bio won't fit everywhere. Write the long one first, then cut.


Where


Length


What to keep


Your website or brokerage page


150 to 250 words


All five parts


LinkedIn About section


Up to 2,600 characters; 100 to 200 words reads best


All five parts, a little more professional


Zillow, Realtor.com or Google Business Profile


80 to 150 words


Who you are, who you help, how you work


Instagram


150 characters


Who you help, where, and one personal note


Email signature or business card


One line


Who you help and where


An Instagram-length version of Dana's bio: "Helping nervous first-time buyers in Oak Park. Softball coach, bad at it. Text me, coffee's on me."


## What to leave out


**Sales volume and rankings.** "$40 million sold" tells a buyer you're busy, not that you'll pick up the phone. If a number matters to your clients, put it on a separate results page.


**A list of designations.** Mention one if it explains who you help (a seniors designation if you work with downsizers). Otherwise, put them in your signature.


**Third person, if it's your own site.** "Dana is a dedicated professional" sounds like a press release. "I" sounds like a person.


**Words every agent uses.** Passionate, dedicated, results-driven, exceptional, seamless. Read your bio and cross them out.


## Do you need IDX search on your website?


IDX (Internet Data Exchange) is the system that lets an agent's website show MLS listings. It's how most agent sites get a property search box.


The case against it is simple. As one broker told us, a website search "will never be as good as Zillow, Redfin or Realtor," and clients already use those. Here's the trade-off as we see it.


With IDX search


Without IDX search


Visitors can search listings on your site


Visitors search on the portals they already use


Can capture leads who register to save searches


Fewer form leads, more direct calls and texts from people who know you


Monthly IDX fees and setup


Simpler, cheaper site


The site looks like every other agent site


The site is about you and your team


Fits a lead-generation business


Fits a referral and relationship business


If most of your business comes from online leads, keep IDX. If it comes from people who already know you or were sent by someone who does, a strong bio page may do more for you than a search box.

A good bio gets you the first call. What happens after that is about remembering people: the softball comment, the parent's house, the sourdough question.

## Who this isn't for


If you're on a large team where the team brand does the selling, your personal bio matters less. Put your effort into the team page and keep your own bio short.


And if your brokerage requires a fixed bio format, work within it. Even a template has room for one real detail.


## FAQ


### What should a realtor bio include?


Who you are and where you live, who you help, one memorable personal detail, how you work with clients and how to reach you. Credentials and sales numbers are optional.


### How long should a real estate agent bio be?


150 to 250 words on your website, 80 to 150 on listing portals and Google, and 150 characters on Instagram. Write the long one first, then cut it down.


### Should a realtor bio be in first or third person?


First person on your own website and social profiles, because it sounds like a real person. Third person is fine for a brokerage roster or a press release if that's the house style.


### What should I put in my realtor Instagram bio?


Who you help, where, and one personal note, in 150 characters. Add a link to your website or contact page.


### Do I need IDX on my real estate website?


Not necessarily. IDX helps if you generate leads from your website. If your business comes from referrals and your sphere, a site built around your bio and your team may serve you better.


### Should I put my sales volume in my bio?


Usually not. It tells people you're successful, not what it's like to work with you. If it matters to your clients, put it on a separate results page.


## The bottom line


Your bio is the one page where a stranger decides whether they'd like you. Write it like you'd introduce yourself at a neighbor's barbecue: who you are, who you help, one detail they'll remember and how to reach you. Leave the sales volume for another page.
